passage:
"Ammi, no go!" Sunaina wrapped both arms round Zeenat's leg at Nani's door.
"I'm going to work, and I'll come back after your nap," said Zeenat, kneeling.
"No! No go!" Sunaina's face crumpled and she sobbed, clinging tighter.
"Here, keep my scarf. It smells like me."
Nani held out her arms. "Come, your cup is ready."
Zeenat kissed her, said, "Bye, see you after nap," and left.
Sunaina wailed at the window, the scarf pressed to her cheek.

qa.q: What did Zeenat give Sunaina before leaving?
qa.a: She gave Sunaina her scarf, saying it smells like her.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina cling to Zeenat's leg and sob?
qa.a: She was scared and upset at being parted from her Ammi, the person who makes her feel safest.

qa.q: Which parts of Zeenat's goodbye were helpful?
qa.a: She told Sunaina simply when she would return, left something comforting and said a clear goodbye instead of sneaking away.

qa.q: What might this goodbye be like for Nani?
qa.a: It may be hard to hear Sunaina wail, but Nani can stay close and comfort her until the crying eases. 🤍

grounding: Shows a toddler's distress at being separated from her main attachment figure.

passage:
Playgroup note on Farhan, Monday, from Rehana.
When his Abbu left this morning, Farhan stood at the door calling "Abbu! Abbu!" and pushed away every toy I offered. I sat on the floor near him, not too close, and said, "Abbu will come after lunch." After a long while he let me hold his hand and we filled cups at the water table. When Abbu came back, Farhan ran and clung to his neck. Tomorrow I'll suggest one short, same goodbye each day.

qa.q: What did Farhan do when his Abbu left?
qa.a: He stood at the door calling "Abbu! Abbu!" and pushed away every toy Rehana offered.

qa.q: What does Farhan clinging to his Abbu's neck at pickup suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he had felt anxious all morning and felt huge relief to have his Abbu back.

qa.q: Why is Rehana's idea of a short, same goodbye each day a good one?
qa.a: A predictable goodbye helps Farhan learn that Abbu always leaves and always comes back, which can slowly ease his distress.

qa.q: How might Farhan's Abbu feel leaving him crying at the door?
qa.a: He might feel guilty and worried, and Rehana's note could reassure him that Farhan was comforted and did settle.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's separation distress at playgroup and a caregiver's gentle support.

passage: Early on market day in the kasba, Asif climbed onto the local bus with sacks of onions to sell in town. From the gate, Parul saw him go. She strained against her Dadi's arms, screaming, one hand stretched toward the bus as it rattled away. For a long time she stood by the gate, sniffling and refusing her roti. At dusk the bus horn sounded. Parul ran barefoot to the gate and would not let go of her Abbu's kurta all evening.

qa.q: What did Asif take to sell in town?
qa.a: He took sacks of onions to sell in town.

qa.q: What does Parul refusing her roti suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was still upset and worried after her Abbu left, too distressed to think about food.

qa.q: How could Asif make market-day partings easier for Parul?
qa.a: He could say a short, warm goodbye before leaving and tell her he will come back with the evening bus, so she knows what to expect.

qa.q: What is it like for Dadi when Parul strains and screams in her arms?
qa.a: It is probably tiring and sad for her, though she can keep comforting Parul and keep her safe until Asif returns.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation anxiety when parted from her father in a small-town setting.

passage: On Monday morning at the nursery in Leeds, Bilal's mum kissed him and turned to leave. Bilal grabbed her coat and screamed, face red and wet. Emeka, his key worker, knelt beside him. 'Mummy's coming back after lunch.' Bilal kicked and reached for the closing door. Emeka held him close by the window, and they waved together. Ten minutes later Bilal was sniffling over the toy trains, still holding Emeka's sleeve.

qa.q: Who is Emeka?
qa.a: Emeka is Bilal's key worker at the nursery.

qa.q: Why did Bilal scream when his mum turned to leave?
qa.a: He was frightened and upset to be apart from her, and did not yet trust that she would come back.

qa.q: What could help Bilal on the next mornings?
qa.a: A short, warm goodbye and the same routine each day, like waving at the window with Emeka, can help him learn she always returns.

qa.q: How might Bilal's mum feel walking away from the door?
qa.a: She may feel sad or guilty hearing him cry, even though she knows he will settle with Emeka.

grounding: Illustrates separation distress in a toddler when parted from his parent, set at a nursery in England.

passage: I'm Elizabeth, and my little brother Yash is almost two. On Mum's night-shift days, I watch what happens. When she picks up her bag, he stops playing and follows her to the door. The moment it shuts, he bangs on it and cries 'Mumma!' until his voice cracks. I carry him to the window so he can see her auto leave. He kicks, then goes quiet on my shoulder. I don't know if he understands she's coming back.

qa.q: What does Yash do the moment the door shuts?
qa.a: He bangs on it and cries 'Mumma!' until his voice cracks.

qa.q: What might Yash be worried about when he follows his mother to the door?
qa.a: He seems worried about being apart from her, and may not yet trust that she will return.

qa.q: What could the older sibling try to make these evenings easier?
qa.a: They could keep a small routine, like the window wave and a favourite toy, and say each time that Mum will come back in the morning.

qa.q: How does the older sibling see Yash's crying?
qa.a: They watch it closely and feel responsible, but they are unsure what Yash understands, which shows care mixed with uncertainty.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation anxiety at a parent's departure, described by an older sibling.

passage: Monday, the first day at the creche: Pema, two, clung to her father's neck and screamed when he left. Vidya, the carer, held her by the window until she cried herself quiet. Wednesday: Pema cried at the door but let Vidya take her hand, and asked "Papa come?" again and again. The next Monday: she waved at the gate, cried for a minute, then went to the sand tray with Vidya.

qa.q: Who held Pema by the window on Monday?
qa.a: Vidya, the carer.

qa.q: What does Pema asking "Papa come?" again and again suggest?
qa.a: She was anxious about being apart and needed to hear her father would come back.

qa.q: What could Vidya and Pema's father do to ease the goodbyes?
qa.a: Keep goodbyes short and the same each day, and have Vidya answer "Papa comes after lunch" every time.

qa.q: What is it like for Pema's father to leave her screaming?
qa.a: It is probably painful and guilt-filled, even if he knows the crying usually passes.

grounding: Shows a toddler's distress at separation easing over the first week at a creche.

passage: At half past eight every morning in their Bengaluru apartment, Uma watched her mother pick up the laptop bag, and her face began to crumple. Today she grabbed the bag strap with both hands and wailed, "No go! No go!" Dolma, the neighbour who minded her, knelt beside her. Her mother kissed her, said, "After nap, I come," and left. Uma sobbed at the closed door until Dolma lifted her to the window to wave.

qa.q: What did Uma grab with both hands?
qa.a: The bag strap.

qa.q: Why did Uma's face begin to crumple when her mother picked up the laptop bag?
qa.a: She knew the bag meant her mother was leaving and felt anxious and upset about being apart.

qa.q: Which part of this goodbye helps Uma, and what could be added?
qa.a: The clear promise "After nap, I come" helps; a short goodbye ritual done the same way every day could help more.

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling while Uma sobs at the door?
qa.a: She may feel sorry for Uma and a little helpless, so she offers the window wave as comfort.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation distress each morning when her mother leaves for work.

passage:
"Ojas, Mumma is going to the wedding for a little while," Gurpreet said, pinning her dupatta. "Nani will play with you."
"No! Mumma!" Ojas wrapped his arms round her leg.
"I'll come back after your milk and one story."
"Mumma stay!"
"Beta, come see the lights," said Nani. The December balcony blinked with fairy lights.
Ojas cried harder and buried his face in her lehenga.
Gurpreet crouched. "Milk, story, Mumma. Say it with me."
"Milk... story... Mumma," he whispered, still sniffing.

qa.q: What will Ojas have before Gurpreet comes back?
qa.a: His milk and one story.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he wrapped his arms round Gurpreet's leg?
qa.a: He felt scared and upset about his mother leaving him.

qa.q: What worked in Gurpreet's goodbye, and why?
qa.a: Giving him a simple sequence to repeat, "milk, story, Mumma", because it helped him predict her return.

qa.q: How might Nani feel as Ojas cries harder at her offer?
qa.a: She might feel a little hurt but patient, knowing he just wants his mother tonight.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation distress on a winter wedding night and a mother giving him a way to predict her return.

passage: Creche note, first day after the summer break. Tenzin (22 months) clung to his father's neck at the gate and screamed when handed to me, reaching back with both arms. He cried at the window for twenty minutes, calling "Pa-la!" I stayed beside him, didn't distract him too quickly, and told him, "Pala comes after lunch." Then he let me hold him while we watered the plants. I'll suggest his father bring a small photo tomorrow. — Mehak

qa.q: How long did Tenzin cry at the window?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he was handed over at the gate?
qa.a: Tenzin felt anxious and distressed at being separated from his father.

qa.q: How did Mehak support Tenzin through the separation?
qa.a: She stayed beside him, told him simply when Pala returns, then gently involved him in watering plants, and plans to use a photo.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's father feel leaving him at the gate?
qa.a: His father probably felt worried and sad, hearing him scream as he left.

grounding: A creche teacher's note records a toddler's separation distress after the summer break and how she supported him.

passage: In wedding season, Preeti had to go to her sister's village for two days. At dawn, when the jeep honked outside their house near Hubballi, Tejas, two, understood. He grabbed the end of her sari and wailed, "Amma no go!" He ran after her, sobbing, while his Ajja held him back. Preeti knelt. "Amma comes back after two sleeps." She tucked her old dupatta into his hands. Tejas pressed it to his face and cried as the jeep pulled away.

qa.q: How long would Preeti be away?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as he grabbed her sari and wailed?
qa.a: Tejas felt distressed and panicky about his mother leaving.

qa.q: What did Preeti do that could help Tejas cope?
qa.a: She knelt, told him simply when she would return, and left her dupatta as a comfort object.

qa.q: How might Ajja feel holding Tejas back?
qa.a: Ajja probably felt sad and sympathetic, but steady, knowing Tejas needs comfort while his mother is away.

grounding: In wedding season, a village toddler is distressed when his mother leaves for two days.

passage: After the Christmas holidays in Madrid, Ingrid took Lucia, twenty months, back to daycare on a cold January morning. For two weeks they had been together every day. At the classroom door Lucia wrapped her arms around her mother's leg and sobbed, "Mamá!" Ingrid crouched, hugged her, and said, "I'll come after nap, like always." Then she left, without sneaking away. Lucia screamed at the glass door. The teacher lifted her up to wave goodbye through it.

qa.q: In which month did Lucia go back to daycare?
qa.a: January.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling at the classroom door?
qa.a: Lucia felt distressed and anxious about being separated from her mother after two weeks together.

qa.q: Why was it good that Ingrid said goodbye instead of sneaking out?
qa.a: A clear goodbye and a promise of when she'll return build trust, even if Lucia cries.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ingrid to hear Lucia screaming at the door?
qa.a: It was probably painful for Ingrid, but she trusted that a clear goodbye was kinder than sneaking away.

grounding: After the Christmas holidays in Spain, a toddler shows separation distress at daycare drop-off.

passage:
I'm Rekha, from the next building. On the first day after the summer holidays, I saw Zubin, not yet two, at the crèche gate with his mother.

When she handed him to the teacher and turned to go, he screamed and stretched both arms after her. He kicked and cried "Mama!" until she was out of sight.

I don't know how long he cried. His mother stood at the corner, wiping her eyes, before she left.

qa.q: What did Zubin cry as his mother left?
qa.a: He cried "Mama!"

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when his mother turned to go?
qa.a: Zubin was distressed and anxious about being parted from his mother.

qa.q: How could the crèche and his mother help Zubin with goodbyes?
qa.a: Keep the goodbye short and warm, and let a familiar teacher comfort him.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother feel wiping her eyes at the corner?
qa.a: His mother was likely sad and worried, finding it hard to leave him crying.

grounding: A neighbour observes a toddler's separation distress at the crèche gate after the summer holidays.

passage:
First monsoon day at daycare: Lokesh, eighteen months, clings to Uday's shirt and screams when he leaves.

Fourth day: he cries at the door, but stops when the teacher shows him the rain on the window.

Tenth day: Uday says, "Papa comes after lunch," and kisses him. Lokesh's lip trembles, but he waves and goes to the sandbox.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh go on the tenth day?
qa.a: He went to the sandbox.

qa.q: How was Lokesh feeling on the tenth day?
qa.a: Lokesh was still a little anxious, with a trembling lip, but brave enough to wave and play.

qa.q: What helped Lokesh with separation over the ten days?
qa.a: A calm routine, Uday's clear promise of when he'd return, and a kind teacher distracting him helped.

qa.q: How might Uday feel on the first day?
qa.a: Uday likely felt sad and guilty leaving Lokesh screaming.

grounding: Over the first monsoon weeks of daycare, a toddler's separation distress slowly eases with a steady goodbye routine.

passage:
In the Diwali crowd at Lajpat Nagar market, Chetan put Gurleen down for a moment to pay for diyas.

She turned and couldn't see him behind the stall. Her face crumpled. She screamed, "Papa! Papa!" and started to run.

Chetan stepped out at once. "I'm here, I'm here." He scooped her up.

Gurleen sobbed into his neck and didn't let go for the rest of the market.

qa.q: Where was the Diwali crowd?
qa.a: The Diwali crowd was at Lajpat Nagar market.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she couldn't see her father?
qa.a: Gurleen was terrified and distressed, afraid he had gone.

qa.q: How could Chetan prevent this next time in a crowd?
qa.a: Keep holding her or keep her in sight in a carrier while paying, so she never loses sight of him.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel after hearing her scream?
qa.a: Chetan was probably shaken and guilty, relieved to hold her again.

grounding: In a crowded Diwali market, a toddler shows separation distress when she briefly loses sight of her father.

passage:
"Mama, no go!" Ira clung to her mother's kurta at the daycare gate.
"I'll be back after your lunch and nap, Ira. I always come back."
"No! Mama stay!"
Her big sister Ishita crouched down. "Ira, look, I'll put my hair clip in your pocket. Keep it for me till Mama comes."
Ira sniffed. "Didi clip?"
"Yes. Keep it safe."
Mama kissed her. "Bye, Ira. See you after nap."
Ira sobbed as the teacher lifted her, but her hand stayed tight on the pocket.

qa.q: What did Ishita put in Ira's pocket?
qa.a: She put her hair clip in Ira's pocket.

qa.q: Why did Ira cling to Mama's kurta at the gate?
qa.a: She felt anxious and scared about being apart from her mother and wanted her to stay.

qa.q: Which part of the goodbye helped Ira, and why?
qa.a: The hair clip gave her something familiar to hold, and Mama's clear promise to return after nap kept the parting short and calm.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita to watch Ira sob?
qa.a: Ishita feels for her little sister and wants to help, so she offers her own clip as comfort.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's separation distress at daycare drop-off and the comfort that helps.
